{{Short description|Differential equation containing derivatives with respect to only one variable}}
[[Image:Parabolic trajectory.svg|right|thumb|250px|alt=parabolic projectile motion showing velocity vector|The [[trajectory]] of a [[projectile]] launched from a [[cannon]] follows a curve determined by an ordinary differential equation that is derived from Newton's second law.]]
{{Differential equations}}

In [[mathematics]], an '''ordinary differential equation''' ('''ODE''') is a [[differential equation]] (DE) dependent on only a single independent [[variable (mathematics)|variable]]. As with any other DE, its unknown(s) consists of one (or more) [[Function (mathematics)|function]](s) and involves the [[derivative]]s of those functions.<ref name="Zill2012">{{cite book|author=Dennis G. Zill|title=A First Course in Differential Equations with Modeling Applications|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=pasKAAAAQBAJ&q=%22ordinary+differential%22|date=15 March 2012|publisher=Cengage Learning|isbn=978-1-285-40110-2|access-date=11 July 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200117230630/https://books.google.com/books?id=pasKAAAAQBAJ&printsec=frontcover#v=snippet&q=%22ordinary%20differential%22&f=false|archive-date=17 January 2020|url-status=live}}</ref> The term "ordinary" is used in contrast with [[partial differential equation|''partial'' differential equations]] (PDEs) which may be with respect to {{em|more than}} one independent variable,<ref>{{cite web|url=http://hsm.stackexchange.com/a/5032/1772|title=What is the origin of the term "ordinary differential equations"? |access-date=2016-07-28|website=hsm.stackexchange.com |publisher=[[Stack Exchange]] }}</ref> and, less commonly, in contrast with [[stochastic differential equations|''stochastic'' differential equations]] (SDEs) where the modeled process is random.<ref>{{cite arXiv|last1=Karras |first1=Tero |last2=Aittala |first2=Miika |last3=Aila |first3=Timo |last4=Laine |first4=Samuli |title=Elucidating the Design Space of Diffusion-Based Generative Models |date=2022 |class=cs.CV |eprint=2206.00364}}</ref>

== Differential equations ==
A [[linear differential equation]] is a differential equation that is defined by a [[linear polynomial]] in the unknown function and its derivatives, that is an [[equation]] of the form 
<math display="block">a_0(x)y +a_1(x)y' + a_2(x)y'' +\cdots +a_n(x)y^{(n)}+b(x)=0,</math>
where <math>a_0(x),\ldots,a_n(x)</math> and <math>b(x)</math> are functions that do not need to be linear, and
<math>y',\ldots, y^{(n)}</math> are the successive derivatives of the unknown function <math>y</math> of the variable <math>x</math>.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Butcher |first=J. C. |date=2000-12-15 |title=Numerical methods for ordinary differential equations in the 20th century |journal=Journal of Computational and Applied Mathematics |series=Numerical Analysis 2000. Vol. VI: Ordinary Differential Equations and Integral Equations |volume=125 |issue=1 |pages=1–29 |doi=10.1016/S0377-0427(00)00455-6 |issn=0377-0427|doi-access=free |bibcode=2000JCoAM.125....1B }}</ref>

Among ordinary differential equations, linear differential equations play a prominent role for several reasons. Most [[elementary function|elementary]] and [[special functions|special]] functions that are encountered in [[physics]] and [[applied mathematics]] are solutions of linear differential equations (see [[Holonomic function]]). When physical phenomena are modeled with non-linear equations, they are generally approximated by linear differential equations for an easier solution. The few non-linear ODEs that can be solved explicitly are generally solved by transforming the equation into an equivalent linear ODE (see, for example [[Riccati equation]]).<ref>{{Cite book |last=Greenberg |first=Michael D. |title=Ordinary differential equations |date=2012 |publisher=Wiley |isbn=978-1-118-23002-2 |location=Hoboken, N.J}}</ref>

Some ODEs can be solved explicitly in terms of known functions and [[antiderivative|integrals]]. When that is not possible, the equation for computing the [[Taylor series]] of the solutions may be useful. For applied problems, [[numerical methods for ordinary differential equations]] can supply an approximation of the solution.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Acton |first=Forman S. |title=Numerical methods that work |date=1990 |publisher=Mathematical Association of America |isbn=978-1-4704-5727-3 |series=Spectrum |location=Washington, D.C}}</ref>

==Background==

Ordinary differential equations (ODEs) arise in many contexts of [[mathematics]] and [[social]] and [[natural science]]s. Mathematical descriptions of change use differentials and derivatives. Various differentials, derivatives, and functions become related via equations, such that a differential equation is a result that describes dynamically changing phenomena, evolution, and variation. Often, quantities are defined as the rate of change of other quantities (for example, derivatives of displacement with respect to time), or [[gradient]]s of quantities, which is how they enter differential equations.<ref>{{cite arXiv |last=Denis |first=Byakatonda |title=An Overview of Numerical and Analytical Methods for solving Ordinary Differential Equations |date=2020-12-10 |class=math.HO |eprint=2012.07558}}</ref>

Specific mathematical fields include [[geometry]] and [[analytical mechanics]]. Scientific fields include much of [[physics]] and [[astronomy]] (celestial mechanics), [[meteorology]] (weather modeling), [[chemistry]] (reaction rates),<ref>Mathematics for Chemists, D.M. Hirst, [[Macmillan Publishers|Macmillan Press]], 1976, (No ISBN) SBN: 333-18172-7</ref> [[biology]] (infectious diseases, genetic variation), [[ecology]] and [[population modeling]] (population competition), [[economics]] (stock trends, interest rates and the market equilibrium price changes).

Many mathematicians have studied differential equations and contributed to the field, including [[Isaac Newton|Newton]], [[Gottfried Leibniz|Leibniz]], the [[Bernoulli family]], [[Riccati]],  [[Alexis Claude Clairaut|Clairaut]], [[d'Alembert]], and [[Euler]].

A simple example is [[Newton's second law]] of motion&mdash;the relationship between the displacement <math>x</math> and the time <math>t</math> of an object under the force <math>F</math>, is given by the differential equation

<math display="block">m \frac{\mathrm{d}^2 x(t)}{\mathrm{d}t^2} = F(x(t))\,</math>

which constrains the [[projectile motion|motion of a particle]] of constant mass <math>m</math>. In general, <math>F</math> is a function of the position <math>x(t)</math> of the particle at time <math>t</math>. The unknown function <math>x(t)</math> appears on both sides of the differential equation, and is indicated in the notation <math>F(x(t))</math>.<ref>{{harvtxt|Kreyszig|1972|p=64}}</ref><ref>{{harvtxt|Simmons|1972|pp=1,2}}</ref><ref>{{harvtxt|Halliday|Resnick|1977|p=78}}</ref><ref>{{harvtxt|Tipler|1991|pp=78–83}}</ref>

==Definitions==
In what follows, <math>y</math> represents an unknown function <math>y=f(x)</math> of the [[variable (mathematics)|variable]] <math>x</math>. The [[notation for differentiation]] varies depending upon the author and upon which notation is most useful for the task at hand. In this context, the [[Leibniz's notation]] 
<math>\frac{dy}{dx},\frac{d^2y}{dx^2},\ldots, \frac{d^ny}{dx^n}</math> is more useful for differentiation and [[Integration (mathematics)|integration]], whereas [[notation for differentiation#Lagrange's notation|Lagrange's notation]] 
<math>y',y'',\ldots,y^{(n)}</math> is more useful for representing [[higher-order derivative]]s compactly, and [[notation for differentiation#Newton's notation|Newton's notation]] <math>(\dot y, \ddot y, \overset{...}{y})</math> is often used in physics for representing derivatives of low order with respect to time.

===General definition===
{{see also|Order of differential equation}}

An ''ordinary differential equation'' of order {{mvar|n}} is an expression  of the form 
<math display="block">F\left(x, y, y', y'',\ \ldots,\ y^{(n)}\right) = 0,</math>
where {{tmath|F}} is a [[function (mathematics)|function]]{{mdash}}typically a [[differentiable function|differentiable]] one{{mdash}} of {{tmath|n+2}} variables, {{tmath|x}} is an [[independent variable]], {{tmath|y}} is an unknown function of {{tmath|x}}, and {{tmath|y', y'', \ldots, y^{(n)} }} are the {{tmath|n}} first derivative of {{tmath|y}}. The term "ordinary" is used to distinguish duch an equation from a [[partial differential equation]]; it is commonly omitted when no confusion may occur, as in the remainder of this article.

By the [[implicit function theorem]], most differential equations can, at least theoretically, be put in the form
<math display="block">y^{(n)}=F\left (x,y,y',\ldots, y^{(n-1)} \right ),</math> which is called an ''[[explicit function|explicit]] differential equation''<ref name="Harper 1976 127"> {{harvtxt|Harper|1976|p=127}}</ref><ref>{{harvtxt|Kreyszig|1972|p=2}}</ref> or a differential equation in ''normal form''.<ref>{{ cite book  | title=Advanced methods for the solution of differential equations | year=1973 | url=https://openlibrary.org/books/OL5522168M | last1=Goldstein | first1=Marvin E. | last2=Braun | first2=Willis H. }}</ref>

There are further classifications:
{{glossary}}
{{term|[[Autonomous system (mathematics)|Autonomous]]}}{{defn|A differential equation is ''autonomous'' if it does not depend on the independent variable {{math|''x''}}.}}
{{term|[[Linear differential equation|Linear]]}}{{defn|
A differential equation is ''linear'' if <math>F</math> can be written as a [[linear combination]] of the dependent variable <math>y</math> and its derivatives; that is, 
<math display="block">y^{(n)} = a_0y +\sum_{i=1}^{n - 1} a_i(x) y^{(i)} + r(x)</math>
where <math>a_i(x)</math> and <math>r(x)</math> are continuous functions of <math>x</math>.<ref name="Harper 1976 127"/><ref name="Kreyszig 1972 24">{{harvtxt|Kreyszig|1972|p=24}}</ref><ref>{{harvtxt|Simmons|1972|p=47}}</ref> The equation has ''constant coefficient'' if all the  <math>a_i(x)</math> are [[constant function]]s. The function <math>r(x)</math> is called the ''nonhomogeneous term'', ''source term'', ''forcing term'', or ''inhomogeneity'', leading to further classification.<ref name="Kreyszig 1972 24"/><ref>{{harvtxt|Harper|1976|p=128}}</ref>}}

{{term|[[Homogeneous differential equation|Homogeneous]]}}{{defn|A linear differential equation is ''homogeneous'' if <math>r(x)=0</math>. In this case, there is always the "[[trivial solution]]" <math>y=0</math>.}}
{{term|[[Homogeneous differential equation#Homogeneous linear differential equations|Nonhomogeneous (or inhomogeneous)]]}}{{defn|A linear differential equation is ''nonhomogeneous'' if <math>r(x)\neq 0</math>. }}

{{term|[[Non-linear differential equation|Non-linear]]}}{{defn|A differential equation that is not linear.}}
{{glossary end}}

===System of ODEs===
{{Main|System of differential equations}}
A number of coupled differential equations form a system of equations. If <math>\mathbf{y}</math> is a vector whose elements are functions; <math>\mathbf{y}(x) = [y_1(x),y_2(x),\ldots, y_m(x)]</math>, and <math>\mathbf{F}</math> is a [[vector-valued function]] of <math>\mathbf{y}</math> and its derivatives, then

<math display="block">\mathbf{y}^{(n)} = \mathbf{F}\left(x,\mathbf{y},\mathbf{y}',\mathbf{y}'',\ldots, \mathbf{y}^{(n-1)} \right)</math>

is an ''explicit system of ordinary differential equations'' of ''order'' <math>n</math> and ''dimension'' <math>m</math>. In [[column vector]] form:

<math display="block">\begin{pmatrix}
y_1^{(n)} \\
y_2^{(n)} \\
\vdots \\
y_m^{(n)}
\end{pmatrix} =

\begin{pmatrix}
f_1 \left (x,\mathbf{y},\mathbf{y}',\mathbf{y}'',\ldots, \mathbf{y}^{(n-1)} \right ) \\
f_2 \left (x,\mathbf{y},\mathbf{y}',\mathbf{y}'',\ldots, \mathbf{y}^{(n-1)} \right ) \\
\vdots \\
f_m \left (x,\mathbf{y},\mathbf{y}',\mathbf{y}'',\ldots, \mathbf{y}^{(n-1)} \right)
\end{pmatrix}</math>

These are not necessarily linear. The ''implicit'' analogue is:

<math display="block">\mathbf{F} \left(x,\mathbf{y},\mathbf{y}',\mathbf{y}'',\ldots, \mathbf{y}^{(n)} \right) = \boldsymbol{0}</math>

where <math>\boldsymbol{0}=(0,0,\ldots,0)</math> is the [[zero vector]]. In matrix form

<math display="block">\begin{pmatrix}
f_1(x,\mathbf{y},\mathbf{y}',\mathbf{y}'',\ldots, \mathbf{y}^{(n)}) \\
f_2(x,\mathbf{y},\mathbf{y}',\mathbf{y}'',\ldots, \mathbf{y}^{(n)}) \\
\vdots \\
f_m(x,\mathbf{y},\mathbf{y}',\mathbf{y}'',\ldots, \mathbf{y}^{(n)})
\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}
0\\
0\\
\vdots\\
0
\end{pmatrix}</math>

For a system of the form <math>\mathbf{F} \left(x,\mathbf{y},\mathbf{y}'\right) = \boldsymbol{0}</math>, some sources also require that the [[Jacobian matrix]] <math>\frac{\partial\mathbf{F}(x,\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v})}{\partial \mathbf{v}}</math> be [[singular matrix|non-singular]] in order to call this an implicit ODE [system]; an implicit ODE system satisfying this Jacobian non-singularity condition can be transformed into an explicit ODE system. In the same sources, implicit ODE systems with a singular Jacobian are termed [[differential algebraic equation]]s (DAEs). This distinction is not merely one of terminology; DAEs have fundamentally different characteristics and are generally more involved to solve than (nonsingular) ODE systems.<ref>{{harvtxt|Kreyszig|1972|p=12}}</ref><ref>{{harvtxt|Ascher|Petzold|1998|p=12}}</ref><ref name="IlchmannReis2014">{{cite book|author1=Achim Ilchmann|author2=Timo Reis|title=Surveys in Differential-Algebraic Equations II|year=2014|publisher=Springer|isbn=978-3-319-11050-9|pages=104–105}}</ref> Presumably for additional derivatives, the [[Hessian matrix]] and so forth are also assumed non-singular according to this scheme,{{citation needed|date=December 2014}} although note that [[#Reduction to a first-order system|any ODE of order greater than one can be (and usually is) rewritten as system of ODEs of first order]],<ref>{{harvtxt|Ascher|Petzold|1998|p=5}}</ref> which makes the Jacobian singularity criterion sufficient for this taxonomy to be comprehensive at all orders.

The behavior of a system of ODEs can be visualized through the use of a [[phase portrait]].

=== Solutions ===
Given a differential equation
<math display="block">F\left(x, y, y', \ldots, y^{(n)} \right) = 0</math>
a function <math>u:I\subset\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}</math>, where <math>I</math> is an interval, is called a ''solution'' or [[integral curve]] for <math>F</math>, if <math>u</math> is <math>n</math>-times differentiable on <math>I</math>, and
<math display="block">F(x,u,u',\ \ldots,\ u^{(n)})=0 \quad x \in I.</math>

Given two solutions <math>u:J\subset\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}</math> and <math>v:I\subset\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}</math>, <math>u</math> is called an ''extension'' of <math>v</math> if <math>I\subset J</math> and
<math display="block">u(x) = v(x) \quad x \in I.\,</math>
A solution that has no extension is called a ''maximal solution''. A solution defined on all of <math>\mathbb{R}</math> is called a ''global solution''.

A ''general solution'' of an <math>n</math>th-order equation is a solution containing <math>n</math> arbitrary independent [[constant of integration|constants of integration]]. A ''particular solution'' is derived from the general solution by setting the constants to particular values, often chosen to fulfill set '[[initial value problem|initial conditions]] or [[boundary value problem|boundary conditions]]'.<ref>{{harvtxt|Kreyszig|1972|p=78}}</ref>  A [[singular solution]] is a solution that cannot be obtained by assigning definite values to the arbitrary constants in the general solution.<ref>{{harvtxt|Kreyszig|1972|p=4}}</ref>

In the context of linear ODE, the terminology ''particular solution'' can also refer to any solution of the ODE (not necessarily satisfying the initial conditions), which is then added to the ''homogeneous'' solution (a general solution of the homogeneous ODE), which then forms a general solution of the original ODE. This is the terminology used in the [[Ordinary differential equation#The guessing method|guessing method]] section in this article, and is frequently used when discussing the [[method of undetermined coefficients]] and [[variation of parameters]].

=== Solutions of finite duration ===

For non-linear autonomous ODEs it is possible under some conditions to develop solutions of finite duration,<ref>{{cite book |author = Vardia T. Haimo |title = 1985 24th IEEE Conference on Decision and Control |chapter = Finite Time Differential Equations |year = 1985 |pages = 1729–1733 |doi = 10.1109/CDC.1985.268832 |s2cid = 45426376 }}</ref> meaning here that from its own dynamics, the system will reach the value zero at an ending time and stays there in zero forever after. These finite-duration solutions can't be analytical functions on the whole real line, and because they will be non-Lipschitz functions at their ending time, they are not included in the uniqueness theorem of solutions of Lipschitz differential equations.

As example, the equation
<math display="block">y'= -\text{sgn}(y)\sqrt{|y|},\,\,y(0)=1</math>
admits the finite duration solution:
<math display="block">y(x)=\frac{1}{4}\left(1-\frac{x}{2}+\left|1-\frac{x}{2}\right|\right)^2</math>

==Theories==

===Singular solutions===
The theory of [[singular solution]]s of ordinary and [[partial differential equation]]s was a subject of research from the time of Leibniz, but only since the middle of the nineteenth century has it received special attention. A valuable but little-known work on the subject is that of [[Louis Houtain|Houtain]] (1854). [[Jean Gaston Darboux|Darboux]] (from 1873) was a leader in the theory, and in the geometric interpretation of these solutions he opened a field worked by various writers, notably [[Felice Casorati (mathematician)|Casorati]] and [[Arthur Cayley|Cayley]]. To the latter is due (1872) the theory of singular solutions of differential equations of the first order as accepted circa 1900.

===Reduction to quadratures===
The primitive attempt in dealing with differential equations had in view a reduction to [[quadrature (mathematics)|quadrature]]s, that is, expressing the solutions in terms of known function and their integrals. This is possible for linear equations with constant coefficients, it appeared in the 19th century that this is generally impossible in other cases. Hence, analysts began the study (for their own) of functions that are solutions of differential equations, thus opening a new and fertile field. [[Cauchy]] was the first to appreciate the importance of this view.  Thereafter, the real question was no longer whether a solution is possible by quadratures, but whether a given differential equation suffices for the definition of a function, and, if so, what are the characteristic properties of such functions.

===Fuchsian theory===
{{main|Frobenius method}}
Two memoirs by [[Lazarus Fuchs|Fuchs]]<ref>''Crelle'', 1866, 1868</ref> inspired a novel approach, subsequently elaborated by Thomé and [[Ferdinand Georg Frobenius|Frobenius]]. (WHO?)Collet was a prominent contributor beginning in 1869. His method for integrating a non-linear system was communicated to Bertrand in 1868. [[Alfred Clebsch|Clebsch]] (1873) attacked the theory along lines parallel to those in his theory of [[Abelian integral]]s. As the latter can be classified according to the properties of the fundamental curve that remains unchanged under a rational transformation, Clebsch proposed to classify the transcendent functions defined by differential equations according to the invariant properties of the corresponding surfaces <math>f=0</math> under rational one-to-one transformations.

===Lie's theory===
From 1870, [[Sophus Lie]]'s work put the theory of differential equations on a better foundation. He showed that the integration theories of the older mathematicians can, using [[Lie group]]s, be referred to a common source, and that ordinary differential equations that admit the same [[infinitesimal transformation]]s present comparable integration difficulties. He also emphasized the subject of [[contact transformation|transformations of contact]].

Lie's group theory of differential equations has been certified, namely: (1) that it unifies the many ad hoc methods known for solving differential equations, and (2) that it provides powerful new ways to find solutions. The theory has applications to both ordinary and partial differential equations.<ref>{{harvtxt|Dresner|1999|p=9}}</ref>

A general solution approach uses the symmetry property of differential equations, the continuous [[infinitesimal transformation]]s of solutions to solutions ([[Lie theory]]). Continuous [[group theory]], [[Lie algebras]], and [[differential geometry]] are used to understand the structure of linear and non-linear (partial) differential equations for generating integrable equations, to find its [[Lax pair]]s, recursion operators, [[Bäcklund transform]], and finally finding exact analytic solutions to DE.

Symmetry methods have been applied to differential equations that arise in mathematics, physics, engineering, and other disciplines.

=== Sturm–Liouville theory ===
{{main|Sturm–Liouville theory}}
Sturm–Liouville theory is a theory of a special type of second-order linear ordinary differential equation. Their solutions are based on [[eigenvalues]] and corresponding [[eigenfunction]]s of linear operators defined via second-order [[System of linear equations|homogeneous linear equations]]. The problems are identified as Sturm–Liouville problems (SLP) and are named after [[Jacques Charles François Sturm|J.&nbsp;C.&nbsp;F.&nbsp;Sturm]] and [[Joseph Liouville|J.&nbsp;Liouville]], who studied them in the mid-1800s. SLPs have an infinite number of eigenvalues, and the corresponding eigenfunctions form a complete, orthogonal set, which makes orthogonal expansions possible. This is a key idea in applied mathematics, physics, and engineering.<ref>Logan, J. (2013). Applied mathematics (4th ed.).</ref> SLPs are also useful in the analysis of certain partial differential equations.

==Existence and uniqueness of solutions==

There are several theorems that establish existence and uniqueness of solutions to [[initial value problem]]s involving ODEs both locally and globally. The two main theorems are

:{| class="wikitable"
|-
! Theorem
! Assumption
! Conclusion
|-
|[[Peano existence theorem]]
||<math>F</math> [[continuous function|continuous]]
||local existence only
|-
|[[Picard–Lindelöf theorem]]
||<math>F</math> [[Lipschitz continuous]]
||local existence and uniqueness
|}

In their basic form both of these theorems only guarantee local results, though the latter can be extended to give a global result, for example, if the conditions of [[Grönwall's inequality]] are met.

Also, uniqueness theorems like the Lipschitz one above do not apply to [[Differential algebraic equation|DAE]] systems, which may have multiple solutions stemming from their (non-linear) algebraic part alone.<ref>{{harvtxt|Ascher|Petzold|1998|p=13}}</ref>

===Local existence and uniqueness theorem simplified===

The theorem can be stated simply as follows.<ref name= "EDEBVP" >Elementary Differential Equations and Boundary Value Problems (4th Edition), W.E. Boyce, R.C. Diprima, Wiley International, John Wiley & Sons, 1986, {{isbn|0-471-83824-1}}</ref> For the equation and initial value problem:
<math display="block"> y' = F(x,y)\,,\quad y_0 = y(x_0)</math>
if <math>F</math> and <math>\partial F/\partial y</math> are continuous in a closed rectangle
<math display="block">R = [x_0-a,x_0+a] \times [y_0-b,y_0+b]</math>
in the <math>x-y</math> plane, where <math>a</math> and <math>b</math> are [[real number|real]] (symbolically: <math>a,b\in\mathbb{R}</math>) and 
<math>\times</math> denotes the [[Cartesian product]], square brackets denote [[interval notation|closed intervals]], then there is an interval
<math display="block">I = [x_0-h,x_0+h] \subset [x_0-a,x_0+a]</math>
for some <math>h\in\mathbb{R}</math> where ''the'' solution to the above equation and initial value problem can be found. That is, there is a solution and it is unique. Since there is no restriction on <math>F</math> to be linear, this applies to non-linear equations that take the form <math>F(x,y)</math>, and it can also be applied to systems of equations.

===Global uniqueness and maximum domain of solution===
When the hypotheses of the Picard–Lindelöf theorem are satisfied, then local existence and uniqueness can be extended to a global result. More precisely:<ref>Boscain; Chitour 2011, p.&nbsp;21</ref>

For each initial condition <math>(x_0,y_0)</math> there exists a unique maximum (possibly infinite) open interval

<math display="block">I_{\max} = (x_-,x_+), x_\pm \in \R \cup \{\pm \infty\}, x_0 \in I_{\max}</math>

such that any solution that satisfies this initial condition is a [[Restriction (mathematics)|restriction]] of the solution that satisfies this initial condition with domain <math>I_\max</math>.

In the case that <math>x_\pm \neq \pm\infty</math>, there are exactly two possibilities

*explosion in finite time: <math>\limsup_{x \to x_\pm} \|y(x)\| \to \infty</math>
*leaves domain of definition: <math>\lim_{x \to x_\pm} y(x)\ \in \partial \bar{\Omega}</math>

where <math>\Omega</math> is the open set in which <math>F</math> is defined, and <math>\partial \bar{\Omega}</math> is its boundary.

Note that the maximum domain of the solution

* is always an interval (to have uniqueness)
* may be smaller than <math>\R</math>
* may depend on the specific choice of <math>(x_0,y_0)</math>.

;Example.

<math display="block">y' = y^2</math>

This means that <math>F(x,y)=y^2</math>, which is <math>C^1</math> and therefore locally Lipschitz continuous, satisfying the Picard–Lindelöf theorem.

Even in such a simple setting, the maximum domain of solution cannot be all <math>\R</math> since the solution is

<math display="block">y(x) = \frac{y_0}{(x_0-x)y_0+1}</math>

which has maximum domain:

<math display="block">\begin{cases}\R & y_0 = 0 \\[4pt] \left (-\infty, x_0+\frac{1}{y_0} \right ) & y_0 > 0 \\[4pt] \left (x_0+\frac{1}{y_0},+\infty \right ) & y_0 < 0 \end{cases}</math>

This shows clearly that the maximum interval may depend on the initial conditions. The domain of <math>y</math> could be taken as being <math>\R \setminus (x_0+ 1/y_0),</math> but this would lead to a domain that is not an interval, so that the side opposite to the initial condition would be disconnected from the initial condition, and therefore not uniquely determined by it.

The maximum domain is not <math>\R</math> because

<math display="block">\lim_{x \to x_\pm} \|y(x)\| \to \infty,</math>

which is one of the two possible cases according to the above theorem.

== Reduction of order ==
Differential equations are usually easier to solve if the [[Differential equation#Order|order]] of the equation can be reduced.

=== Reduction to a first-order system === <!-- Redirect [[Stiff equation]] links here -->
Any explicit differential equation of order <math>n</math>,

<math display="block">F\left(x, y, y', y'',\ \ldots,\ y^{(n-1)}\right) = y^{(n)}</math>

can be written as a system of <math>n</math> first-order differential equations by defining a new family of unknown functions

<math display="block">y_i = y^{(i-1)}.\!</math>

for <math>i=1,2,\ldots,n</math>. The <math>n</math>-dimensional system of first-order coupled differential equations is then

<math display="block">\begin{array}{rcl}
  y_1'&=&y_2\\
  y_2'&=&y_3\\
  &\vdots&\\
  y_{n-1}'&=&y_n\\
  y_n'&=&F(x,y_1,\ldots,y_n).
\end{array}
</math>

more compactly in vector notation:

<math display="block">\mathbf{y}'=\mathbf{F}(x,\mathbf{y})</math>

where
<math display="block">\mathbf{y}=(y_1,\ldots,y_n),\quad \mathbf{F}(x,y_1,\ldots,y_n)=(y_2,\ldots,y_n,F(x,y_1,\ldots,y_n)).</math>

==Summary of exact solutions==
<!--Please leave the tables alone. If a table format is really disliked then instead of simply deleting it - expand into prose. For now they are there to summarize some common forms of equations and their solutions. Details are in the other articles. -->

Some differential equations have solutions that can be written in an exact and closed form. Several important classes are given here.

In the table below, <math>P(x)</math>, <math>Q(x)</math>, <math>P(y)</math>, <math>Q(y)</math>, and <math>M(x,y)</math>, <math>N(x,y)</math> are any [[integrable]] functions of <math>x</math>, <math>y</math>; <math>b</math> and <math>c</math> are real given constants; <math>C_1,C_2,\ldots</math> are arbitrary constants ([[complex number|complex]] in general). The differential equations are in their equivalent and alternative forms that lead to the solution through integration.

In the integral solutions, <math>\lambda</math> and <math>\varepsilon</math> are dummy variables of integration (the continuum analogues of indices in [[summation]]), and the notation <math>\int^x F(\lambda)\, d\lambda</math> just means to integrate <math>F(\lambda)</math> with respect to <math>\lambda</math>, then ''after'' the integration substitute <math>\lambda=x</math>, without adding constants (explicitly stated).

=== Separable equations ===
{| class="wikitable"
|-
! scope="col" | Differential equation
! scope="col" | Solution method
! scope="col" | General solution
|-
| First-order, separable in <math>x</math> and <math>y</math> (general case, see below for special cases)<ref name="MHFT">Mathematical Handbook of Formulas and Tables (3rd edition), S. Lipschutz, M. R. Spiegel, J. Liu, Schaum's Outline Series, 2009, ISC_2N 978-0-07-154855-7</ref>

<math>\begin{align}
  P_1(x)Q_1(y) + P_2(x)Q_2(y)\,\frac{dy}{dx} &= 0 \\
         P_1(x)Q_1(y)\,dx + P_2(x)Q_2(y)\,dy &= 0
\end{align}</math>
| Separation of variables (divide by <math>P_2Q_1</math>).
| <math> \int^x \frac{P_1(\lambda)}{P_2(\lambda)}\,d\lambda + \int^y \frac{Q_2(\lambda)}{Q_1(\lambda)}\,d\lambda = C </math>
|-
| First-order, separable in <math>x</math><ref name= "EDEBVP" />
<math>\begin{align}
  \frac{dy}{dx} &= F(x) \\
             dy &= F(x) \, dx
\end{align}</math>
| Direct integration.
| <math>y= \int^x F(\lambda) \, d\lambda + C </math>
|-
| First-order, autonomous, separable in <math>y</math><ref name= "EDEBVP" />

<math>\begin{align}
  \frac{dy}{dx} &= F(y) \\
             dy &= F(y) \, dx
\end{align}</math>
| [[Separation of variables]] (divide by <math>F</math>).
| <math>x=\int^y \frac{d\lambda}{F(\lambda)} + C</math>
|-
| First-order, separable in <math>x</math> and <math>y</math><ref name= "EDEBVP" />

<math>\begin{align}
  P(y)\frac{dy}{dx} + Q(x) &= 0 \\
       P(y)\,dy + Q(x)\,dx &= 0
\end{align}</math>
| Integrate throughout.
| <math>\int^y P(\lambda)\, d\lambda + \int^x Q(\lambda)\,d\lambda = C</math>
|}

=== General first-order equations ===
{| class="wikitable"
|-
! scope="col" | Differential equation
! scope="col" | Solution method
! scope="col" | General solution
|-
| First-order, homogeneous<ref name="EDEBVP" />

<math>\frac{dy}{dx} = F \left( \frac y x \right ) </math>
| Set ''y = ux'', then solve by separation of variables in ''u'' and ''x''.
| <math> \ln (Cx) = \int^{y/x} \frac{d\lambda}{F(\lambda) - \lambda} </math>
|-
| First-order, separable<ref name= "MHFT" />

<math>\begin{align}
  yM(xy) + xN(xy)\,\frac{dy}{dx} &= 0 \\
         yM(xy)\,dx + xN(xy)\,dy &= 0
\end{align}</math>

| Separation of variables (divide by <math>xy</math>).
|
<math> \ln (Cx) = \int^{xy} \frac{N(\lambda)\,d\lambda}{\lambda [N(\lambda)-M(\lambda)] } </math>

If <math>N=M</math>, the solution is <math>xy=C</math>.
|-
| [[Exact differential equation|Exact differential]], first-order<ref name= "EDEBVP" />

<math>\begin{align}
  M(x,y) \frac{dy}{dx} + N(x,y) &= 0 \\
        M(x,y)\,dy + N(x,y)\,dx &= 0
\end{align}</math>

where <math> \frac{\partial M}{\partial y} = \frac{\partial N}{\partial x} </math>

| Integrate throughout.
| <math>\begin{align}
  F(x,y) &= \int^x M(\lambda,y)\,d\lambda + \int^y Y(\lambda)\,d\lambda \\
         &= \int^y N(x,\lambda)\,d\lambda + \int^x X(\lambda)\,d\lambda=C
\end{align}</math>
where
<math display="block">Y(y)= N(x,y)-\frac{\partial}{\partial y}\int^x M(\lambda,y)\,d\lambda</math> and
<math display="block">X(x)= M(x,y)-\frac{\partial}{\partial x}\int^y N(x,\lambda)\,d\lambda </math>
|-
| [[Inexact differential equation|Inexact differential]], first-order<ref name= "EDEBVP" />

<math>\begin{align}
  M(x,y) \frac{dy}{dx} + N(x,y) &= 0 \\
        M(x,y)\,dy + N(x,y)\,dx &= 0
\end{align}</math>

where <math> \frac{\partial M}{\partial y} \neq \frac{\partial N}{\partial x} </math>
| [[Integration factor]] <math>\mu(x,y)</math> satisfying

<math> \frac{\partial (\mu M)}{\partial y} = \frac{\partial (\mu N)}{\partial x} </math>
| If <math>\mu(x,y)</math> can be found in a suitable way, then

<math>\begin{align}
  F(x,y) = &\int^x \mu(\lambda,y)M(\lambda,y)\,d\lambda + \int^y Y(\lambda)\,d\lambda \\
         = &\int^y \mu(x,\lambda)N(x,\lambda)\,d\lambda + \int^x X(\lambda)\,d\lambda = C
\end{align}</math>

where <math display="block">Y(y)= N(x,y)-\frac{\partial}{\partial y}\int^x \mu (\lambda,y)M(\lambda,y)\,d\lambda</math>
and <math display="block">X(x)= M(x,y)-\frac{\partial}{\partial x}\int^y \mu (x,\lambda)N(x,\lambda)\,d\lambda</math>
|}

=== General second-order equations ===
{| class="wikitable"
|-
! scope="col" | Differential equation
! scope="col" | Solution method
! scope="col" | General solution
|-
| Second-order, autonomous<ref>Further Elementary Analysis, R. Porter, G.Bell & Sons (London), 1978, {{isbn|0-7135-1594-5}}</ref>

<math>\frac{d^2y}{dx^2} = F(y) </math>
| Multiply both sides of equation by <math>2 \frac{dy}{dx} </math>, substitute {{nowrap|<math>2 \frac{dy}{dx} \frac{d^2y}{dx^2} = \frac{d}{dx} \left(\frac{dy}{dx}\right)^2 = 2 \frac{dy}{dx} F(y) </math>,}} then integrate twice.
| <math> x = \pm \int^y \frac{ d \lambda}{\sqrt{2 \int^\lambda F(\varepsilon) \, d \varepsilon + C_1}} + C_2 </math>
|}

=== Linear to the <span style="font-style:italic; font-family:serif;">n</span>th order equations ===
{| class="wikitable"
|-
! scope="col" | Differential equation
! scope="col" | Solution method
! scope="col" | General solution
|-
| First-order, linear, inhomogeneous, function coefficients<ref name="EDEBVP" />

<math>\frac{dy}{dx} + P(x)y = Q(x)</math>

| Integrating factor: <math>e^{\int^x P(\lambda)\,d\lambda}.</math>
| <math>y = e^{- \int^x P(\lambda) \, d\lambda}\left[\int^x e^{\int^\lambda P(\varepsilon) \, d\varepsilon}Q(\lambda) \, d\lambda +C \right]</math>
|-
|Second-order, linear, inhomogeneous, function coefficients
<math>\frac{d^2y}{dx^2}+2p(x)\frac{dy}{dx}+\left(p(x)^2+p'(x)\right)y=q(x) </math>
|Integrating factor: <math>e^{\int^x P(\lambda)\,d\lambda}</math>
|<math>y = e^{- \int^x P(\lambda) \, d\lambda}\left[\int^x\left(\int^\xi e^{\int^\lambda P(\varepsilon) \, d\varepsilon}Q(\lambda) \, d\lambda \right)d\xi +C_1x+C_2\right]</math>
|-
| Second-order, linear, inhomogeneous, constant coefficients<ref name="MMPE">Mathematical methods for physics and engineering, K.F. Riley, M.P. Hobson, S.J. Bence, Cambridge University Press, 2010, ISC_2N 978-0-521-86153-3</ref>

<math>\frac{d^2y}{dx^2} + b\frac{dy}{dx} + cy = r(x)</math>
| Complementary function <math>y_c</math>: assume <math>y_c(x)=e^{\alpha x}</math>, substitute and solve polynomial in <math>\alpha</math>, to find the [[linearly independent]] functions <math>e^{\alpha_j x}</math>.

Particular integral <math>y_p</math>: in general the [[method of variation of parameters]], though for very simple <math>r(x)</math> inspection may work.<ref name="EDEBVP" />
| <math>y = y_c + y_p</math>

If <math>b^2>4c</math>, then

<math>y_c = C_1e^{ -\frac x2\,\left(b + \sqrt{b^2 - 4c}\right)} + C_2e^{-\frac x2\,\left(b - \sqrt{b^2 - 4c}\right)}</math>

If <math>b^2=4c</math>, then

<math>y_c = (C_1x + C_2)e^{-\frac{bx}{2}}</math>

If <math>b^2<4c</math>, then

<math>y_c = e^{ -\frac{bx}{2}} \left[ C_1 \sin\left( x\,\frac{\sqrt{4c-b^2}}{2}\right) + C_2\cos\left( x\,\frac{\sqrt{4c-b^2}}{2}\right)\right]</math>
|-
|<math>n</math>th-order, linear, inhomogeneous, constant coefficients<ref name="MMPE" />

<math> \sum_{j=0}^n b_j \frac{d^j y}{dx^j} = r(x)</math>
| Complementary function <math>y_c</math>: assume <math>y_c(x)=e^{\alpha x}</math>, substitute and solve polynomial in <math>\alpha</math>, to find the [[linearly independent]] functions <math>e^{\alpha_j x}</math>.

Particular integral <math>y_p</math>: in general the [[method of variation of parameters]], though for very simple <math>r(x)</math> inspection may work.<ref name="EDEBVP" />
|<math>y = y_c + y_p</math>

Since <math>\alpha_j</math> are the solutions of the [[polynomial]] of [[Degree of a polynomial|degree]] <math>n</math>: <math display="inline"> \prod_{j=1}^n ( \alpha - \alpha_j) = 0 </math>, then:
for <math>\alpha_j</math> all different,
<math display="block"> y_c = \sum_{j=1}^n C_j e^{\alpha_j x} </math>
for each root <math>\alpha_j</math> repeated <math>k_j</math> times,
<math display="block"> y_c = \sum_{j=1}^n \left( \sum_{\ell=1}^{k_j} C_{j,\ell} x^{\ell-1}\right )e^{\alpha_j x}</math>
for some <math>\alpha_j</math> complex, then setting <math>\alpha_j = \chi_j + i\gamma_j</math>, and using [[Euler's formula]], allows some terms in the previous results to be written in the form
<math display="block"> C_j e^{\alpha_j x} = C_j e^{\chi_j x}\cos(\gamma_j x + \varphi_j)</math>
where <math>\varphi_j</math> is an arbitrary constant (phase shift).
|}

==Guessing solutions==
{{See also|1=Ansatz|2=Glossary_of_mathematical_jargon#by_inspection|label2=Proof by inspection}}

If an ODE satisfies the conditions of the [[Picard-Lindelof theorem]], then it has a unique solution, and it suffices to correctly ''guess'' and verify that solution. Several less-than-completely rigorous
methods to guess the solution exist, most notably the [[method of undetermined coefficients]].<ref>{{cite book |last1=Hubbard |first1=John H. |last2=West |first2=Beverly H. |title=Differential equations: a dynamical systems approach |date=1991 |publisher=Springer-Verlag |location=New York |isbn=0-387-97286-2 |pages=72-76}}</ref>

== Software for ODE solving ==
* [[Maxima (software)|Maxima]], an open-source [[computer algebra system]].
* [[COPASI]], a free ([[Artistic License|Artistic License 2.0]]) software package for the integration and analysis of ODEs.
* [[MATLAB]], a technical computing application (MATrix LABoratory)
* [[GNU Octave]], a high-level language, primarily intended for numerical computations.
* [[Scilab]], an open source application for numerical computation.
* [[Maple (software)|Maple]], a proprietary application for symbolic calculations. 
* [[Mathematica]], a proprietary application primarily intended for symbolic calculations. 
* [[SymPy]], a Python package that can solve ODEs symbolically
* [[Julia (programming language)]], a high-level language primarily intended for numerical computations.
* [[SageMath]], an open-source application that uses a Python-like syntax with a wide range of capabilities spanning several branches of mathematics.
* [[SciPy]], a Python package that includes an ODE integration module.
* [[Chebfun]], an open-source package, written in [[MATLAB]], for computing with functions to 15-digit accuracy.
* [[GNU R]], an open source computational environment primarily intended for statistics, which includes packages for ODE solving.
